title: Three σ-algebras
promptMarkdown:
Let $X$ be a set.

1. Let $\{A_1,\dots,A_n\}$ be a partition of $X$ into $n\ge1$ nonempty sets. Describe the σ-algebra $\sigma(\{A_1,\dots,A_n\})$ generated by the blocks explicitly, prove that your description is correct, and determine how many sets it contains.
2. Let $X$ be uncountable and $\mathcal M_c=\{A\subset X: A\text{ is countable or }X\setminus A\text{ is countable}\}$. Prove that $\mathcal M_c$ is a σ-algebra, and prove that $\mathcal M_c=\sigma(\{\{x\}:x\in X\})$, the σ-algebra generated by the singletons.
3. Let $X$ be infinite and $\mathcal F=\{A\subset X: A\text{ is finite or }X\setminus A\text{ is finite}\}$. Show that $\mathcal F$ satisfies (σ1) and (σ2) and is closed under finite unions, but is **not** a σ-algebra: exhibit a sequence in $\mathcal F$ whose union is not in $\mathcal F$, and name the axiom that fails.
hintLadder: Any σ-algebra containing each block contains every finite union of blocks. Is the family of all unions of blocks already a σ-algebra? Check complements and countable unions.
For (σ3) in part 2, split into two cases: every $A_i$ is countable, or some $A_j$ has countable complement. In the second case use $\big(\bigcup_i A_i\big)^c\subset A_j^c$.
To show $\mathcal M_c\subset\sigma(\text{singletons})$, write a countable set as a countable union of singletons and a co-countable set as the complement of one.
In part 3, pick a countably infinite subset $\{x_1,x_2,\dots\}\subset X$ and take every other point.

deterministicChecks.description: the σ-algebra generated by a partition into n blocks has 2^n elements
particular values of n are not a proof for all n

criteria.criterion: The generated σ-algebra is identified as the family of unions of sub-collections of blocks, shown to be a σ-algebra containing the blocks and contained in any σ-algebra containing them, with the count 2^n justified (distinct index sets give distinct unions because the blocks are nonempty).

levels.label: met
levels.description: Both inclusions and the count with its reason.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: Description and count stated; one inclusion or the distinctness argument missing.

criteria.criterion: (σ1), (σ2) and (σ3) verified for M_c, with the case split for countable unions made explicit.

levels.label: met
levels.description: All three axioms, case split explicit.

criteria.criterion: Both inclusions between M_c and σ(singletons) argued: singletons lie in M_c, and every countable or co-countable set is built from singletons by countable unions and one complement.
(σ1), (σ2) and closure under finite unions checked for F; an explicit sequence in F with union outside F exhibited (infinite with infinite complement) and (σ3) named as the failing axiom.

levels.label: met
levels.description: Explicit witness, verification that it is outside F, axiom named.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: Failure asserted with a vague witness, or axiom not named.

levels.label: not met
levels.description: Missing or claims F is a σ-algebra.

checkExamples.label: general count with LaTeX
checkExamples.text: Every set in the generated σ-algebra is a union of blocks: the unions of blocks form a σ-algebra containing each $A_i$ (the complement of a union over an index set is the union over the complementary index set, and any union of unions of blocks is again a union of blocks), and every σ-algebra containing the blocks contains all their finite unions. Distinct index sets give distinct unions because the blocks are nonempty, so for every $n$ there are exactly $2^n$ sets.

checkExamples.label: count without the formula
checkExamples.text: The generated σ-algebra consists of all unions of blocks, so it has 2n elements.

checkExamples.label: instances only
checkExamples.text: For n=1 the σ-algebra has 2 sets, for n=2 it has 4 sets and for n=3 it has 8 sets, so the count is right.
